newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Falling yen to pressure S.Korean shipbuilders in 97.
newsitem.headline: Falling yen to pressure S.Korean shipbuilders in 97.

text.p: South Korean shipbuilders will face more choppy water this year after posting dismal results in 1996, mainly as a result of the sharply falling Japanese yen, analysts said on Monday.
Falling ship prices, slowing demand for bulk and container carriers and other poorly performing divisions could also drag down earnings, they added.

"A popular misconception is that because the Korean won has been depreciating against the dollar fairly rapidly, exporters should gain a lot of advantages," said Kim Chong-hyuk, an analyst with Ssangyong Investment and Securities Co.
"But won versus the yen, the won has actually appreciated."
The nation's listed shipbuilders, Samsung Heavy Industry Ltd, Hanjin Heavy Industries Co and Daewoo Heavy Industries Ltd saw, or expect to see, 1996 earnings plunge.

Samsung Heavy, an affiliate of Samsung Group, posted a net loss of 294.6 billion won ($335 million) in 1996, compared to a net profit of 41.2 billion a year earlier, while sales rose to 3.26 trillion from 2.92 trillion.
Hanjin's net profit fell to 3.2 billion won on sales of 600.5 billion, from 13.2 billion on turnover of 541.8 billion reported in 1995.
Daewoo, an affiliate of the Daewoo Group, forecast its net profit had fallen to 75 billion won last year from 129.5 billion in 1995.
It estimated its sales were around 5.15 trillion won, sharply up from 3.96 trillion won. Final figures would be available after its shareholders' meeting later this month, the company said.

The won, pressured by the nation's widening trade deficit and the dollar's bullishness on world markets, has lost nearly 13.6 percent against the dollar since the start of 1996. Then the dollar was trading at 774.70 won.
But the Japanese yen lost nearly 18 percent to trade at around 123.60 yen against the dollar on Monday from around 105 yen early last year.
"Since 1993, shipbuilding prices have continued to decline globally, reflecting toughening competition and faster growth of supply than demand," said analyst Vince Kim of Jardine Fleming Securities.
In January, South Korea, the world's second largest ship exporter after Japan, won orders totalling 230,500 gross tonnes, a 0.95 percent decline from a year earlier.
Japanese shipyards received 17 ship orders from foreign companies, totalling 523,030 gross registered tonnes. This was down 0.4 percent.
Ssangyong's Kim forecast an operating revenue of 3.6 trillion won for Samsung Heavy in 1997. Further analysis would be needed before he could predict its net profit, he added.
For Hanjin Heavy, he saw a net loss of five to six billion won on turnover of 650-660 billion.
Daewoo was seen posting a net profit of 40-50 billion, on sales of 5.4 trillion, he said.
South Korean shipmakers are also being hit by decelerating demand for bulk carriers and container ships since orders for these peaked in 1995.
"You also have to remember that shipbuilding accounts for only 30-40 percent of (Samsung and Daewoo's) business now," said Ssangyong's Kim.

"So the real question is what will be happening to the other 60-70 percent? None of the other divisions is going to show a recovery in 1997. In fact, in the case of Daewoo, shipbuilding is going to be the brighter spot."
